docs.title: CLS-Open #8 — Linux, Git and Reproducible Workflows for Bioinformatics
docs.text:
A beginner course that treats the command line, version control and workflow files as scientific instruments, not incidental plumbing.

Honest version status — v0.1.0

Module 1 is complete (13-part lesson, executed notebook, two guided practicals, assignment, challenge, quiz, instructor pack). Modules 2–9 are specified but not yet written — see Roadmap. Nothing in this repository is a placeholder pretending to be a lesson.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text: If you are… Go to a life-science student with no terminal experience Installation → Module 1 a researcher who "uses the command line a bit" Prerequisites self-check → Practical 01 an instructor Instructor pack (12/24/36-hour plans, marking load) a reviewer or contributor Validation · Limitations · References looking for the software pip install -e . then bioflow --help

docs.title: What makes this repository different
docs.text:
1. Every number is recomputed by CI. The notebooks execute on every push; if an example breaks, the build fails.
  2. Disagreement is taught, not hidden. The record-count trap (200 vs 204) is a lesson, not an erratum.
  3. Two real bugs found while writing the material are documented — one in our own pipeline engine, one in an "obvious" GC one-liner — because a course that shows only clean code teaches the wrong instinct.
  4. Validation against an independent implementation (Biopython) with published numbers, not a claim.
  5. Assessment that instructors can actually use: rubrics, answer keys, common wrong answers, marking-load estimates.

docs.title: Standard install (5 minutes)
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/cls-open/linux-git-for-bioinformatics.git
cd linux-git-for-bioinformatics

python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate          # Windows (WSL2): source .venv/bin/activate

pip install -e ".[dev]"
bioflow --version
python -m pytest -q                # expect: 65 passed

docs.title: Verify your install (do not skip)
docs.text:
python scripts/make_sample_data.py   # regenerates the simulated datasets (deterministic)
bioflow stats datasets/sample/reads.fastq

Expected:

records         : 200
total bases     : 12000
GC              : 60.4%  (ambiguous bases excluded)
N50             : 60
mean Phred      : 30.46

If those five numbers match, your environment is correct. If they do not, stop and fix it — every later lesson depends on them.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text: Use WSL2 (wsl --install then sudo apt install python3-venv build-essential). Git Bash is not sufficient: awk, sort and grep behave differently enough to produce confusing results, and /usr/bin/time is absent.

docs.title: No-install route
docs.text:
• notebooks/01_unix_mindset.ipynb runs in a free Colab/JupyterHub instance. Upload the repository (it is <1 MB), then run the notebook from the repository root.
  • A container recipe is in docs/limitations.md §containers (Docker/Podman) — not required for any graded exercise.

docs.title: Self-check before starting
docs.text:
Answer without looking anything up (answers in quiz):

  1. What does > do to the target file before the command runs?
  2. How many lines is one FASTQ record?
  3. What is the file descriptor number for stderr?

Two out of three correct → start at Module 1 and move quickly. Fewer → start at Module 1 and do both practicals.

docs.title: After this repository
docs.text:
You will be able to run real analyses (Modules 7–8), but you will not yet know what to analyse. That is #4 and #11's job. The intended sequence is:

  1. #8 (this repo) — survive the machine.
  2. #4 bioinformatics-foundations — sequence to function, by implementing the algorithms.
  3. #11 genomics-and-ngs-analysis — real data, real QC gates, real confounders.
  4. #15 advanced-bioinformatics-and-ai-research — benchmark and audit published models.

docs.title: Limitations and known failure cases
docs.text: This page is a requirement of the repository, not an afterthought. A tool without a limitations statement is a tool you cannot safely use.

docs.title: Software (bioflow 0.1.0)
docs.text: Limitation Consequence Workaround Sequential execution only --jobs N is accepted and ignored (with a warning on stderr) Use Snakemake/Nextflow for parallelism; Module 7 explains why they exist shell=True execution Pipeline YAML is executable code; a malicious pipeline can do anything your user can Only run pipelines you have read; treat pipeline files like source code No containers No isolation, no reproducible toolchain Use Docker/Singularity; see Module 4 No wildcard/pattern rules You must enumerate every file Snakemake's expand/wildcards; Module 7 Cache key = command string + input content Changing an environment (e.g. tool version) does not invalidate the cache Also hash versions.txt as an input, or rm -rf .bioflow stats holds all lengths in memory N50/histogram memory grows with record count Challenge 01 asks you to fix this properly FASTA/FASTQ only No GFF/VCF/BAM/SAM Module 7+; or use pysam, bcftools Single-line FASTQ assumed for NR%4 examples Wrapped FASTQ breaks the lesson's one-liners (the parser is fine) Use bioflow stats; treat wrapping as an error No Windows-native support Paths and POSIX tools differ WSL2 Phred+64 not auto-detected Old Solexa/Illumina data would be mis-scored Out of scope; detect manually before use

docs.title: Educational limitations
docs.text:
• Modules 2–9 are specified, not written (see roadmap). Using this repository as a 24–36 hour course today means supplementing those modules yourself.
  • The datasets are simulated; learners do not meet adapter contamination, index hopping, or batching.
  • No cohort data exists yet: learning gains are not measured, and this repository makes no claim that it improves learning outcomes. Any such claim will require ethics approval, consent and pre/post instruments — see the publication strategy in the initiative's initiation report.
  • English only (v0.1). Translation is permitted and encouraged under CC BY 4.0.
  • Accessibility: colour-blind-safe palettes and alt text are used in figures; screen-reader testing of the docs site has not been done. Reports of accessibility problems are treated as high-priority bugs.

docs.title: Two bugs found while writing this material (kept as lessons)
docs.text:
1. str.format and shell braces. Rendering {inputs} with Python's str.format raised KeyError on awk '{if (n) print n}'. Fixed by explicit token replacement; regression test test_awk_braces_survive_rendering.
  2. gsub mutates $0. The "obvious" GC one-liner computed lengths after substituting G/C out of the line, producing GC = 152%. Both versions are in the notebook, because the failure is more instructive than the fix.

Both are documented rather than quietly patched because a course that shows only working code teaches learners to distrust their own (correct) suspicion that something is wrong.

docs.title: Required
docs.text:
• You can create, move and delete files in a graphical file manager.
  • You know what DNA/RNA/protein are, and that DNA is double-stranded.
  • You can read a table of numbers and say what a column means.

That is all. There is no programming prerequisite: this repository is the entry point of the CLS-Open pathway.

docs.title: Helpful but not required
docs.text:
• Any prior exposure to statistics (mean, median, standard deviation).
  • Any prior use of a spreadsheet for scientific data.
  • English reading proficiency (the material is English; translations are welcome under CC BY 4.0).

docs.title: Self-assessment (10 minutes)
docs.text:
Try these in a terminal. It is completely fine if you cannot do any of them.

pwd                 # where am I?
ls -la              # what is here, including hidden files?
cd /tmp && cd -     # move and return
echo "hello" > a.txt && cat a.txt

If you can do all four, you will finish Module 1 in ~2 hours. If none, budget 4–5 hours and do Practical 01 twice.

docs.text:

  • Statistics choices for biological designs (that is #6).
  • Any specific genomics pipeline biology (#11).

Stating this is itself a requirement of the course: knowing what a tool does not do is part of using it correctly.

docs.title: How to check a reference in this repository
docs.text:
# Crossref resolution for a DOI
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" "https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1093/bib/bbad375"

A 200 means the DOI resolves in Crossref; it does not prove the claim made about the paper. That is a separate check performed by reading the source.

docs.title: Policy
docs.text: No reference appears in a CLS-Open repository unless it has been opened and its content confirmed to support the sentence citing it. If a citation is found to be wrong, it is corrected in a CHANGELOG entry naming the file and the lesson — silently editing citations is itself a reproducibility failure.

docs.title: Validation — what was checked, how, and with what result
docs.text: A tool is not validated because it has tests. It is validated when its outputs are compared against something independent and the comparison is published. This page records both.

docs.title: 1. Cross-validation against Biopython (external implementation)
docs.text:
Command (reproduce with scripts/validate_against_biopython.py, requires pip install biopython):

Quantity bioflow Biopython (SeqIO) Agreement FASTQ records 200 200 exact FASTQ total bases 12 000 12 000 exact FASTQ GC% 60.4 60.4 exact to 2 dp FASTQ mean Phred 30.46 30.46 exact to 2 dp FASTQ per-position means — — max abs diff 5.0×10⁻³ (rounding to 2 dp) FASTA records 12 12 exact FASTA total bases 1 039 1 039 exact FASTA N50 102 102 exact

Date: 2026-11-06. Datasets: datasets/sample/* (simulated, fixed seed). What this establishes: our parser and statistics agree with the field's reference library on the shipped data. What it does not establish: correctness on adversarial inputs (that is the unit-test suite's job) or correctness of definitions (both implementations could be wrong the same way — hence the definitions are stated in the module and computed by hand in tests/test_stats.py).

docs.title: 2. Hand-computed unit tests
docs.text: tests/test_stats.py contains cases whose expected values are derived by hand in the comments, e.g. lengths [10, 9, 2] → total 21 → half 10.5 → cumulative 10, then 19 ≥ 10.5 → N50 = 9. These catch definitional errors that cross-validation cannot.

docs.title: 3. Behavioural tests for the pipeline engine (65 tests total)
docs.text: Area Tests Key properties proven Parsing 13 format detection, multi-line FASTA, gzip, malformed FASTQ raises, length-mismatch raises Statistics 13 GC definition, N50 definition, Phred offset, empty input, generator streaming DAG + execution 15 topological order, cycle detection, unsatisfiable input detected before running, failing step stops the pipeline, missing declared output is a failure Caching 4 second run skips, changed input reruns, deleted output reruns, stamps record hashes CLI 20 real argv/exit codes, JSON schema, error paths, --dry-run, --jobs honesty warning

docs.title: 4. Reproducibility of the material itself
docs.text:
• notebooks/01_unix_mindset.ipynb executes end-to-end with 0 errors; it is re-executed in CI on every push.
  • scripts/make_figures.py regenerates all three figures from data; CI fails if the figures change without a data or code change being committed.
  • scripts/make_sample_data.py regenerates the datasets byte-identically (fixed seed).

docs.title: 5. Known limits of this validation
docs.text:
1. The datasets are simulated, so the validation says nothing about real instrument behaviour (quality-score drift, adapters, GC bias).
  2. Biopython agreement is on 200 records × 60 bp — small; a large-file cross-check is part of Challenge 01.
  3. No external reviewer has yet audited this repository. When one does, their name and comments will be recorded here only with their consent.
  4. Performance is not benchmarked beyond the memory demonstration in Practical 02; Challenge 01 requires real numbers.

docs.title: Assignment 01 — Reproducibility audit of a shell-based analysis
docs.text: Level: L3 (independent) · Weight: 15% of the course · Time: 3–4 hours · Due: end of Module 2

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
A collaborator sends you this, claiming they "did the QC":

fastqc *.fastq -o ~/qc
cat *.fastq | cut -d' ' -f1 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -20 > duplicates.txt
multiqc ~/qc -o ~/qc/summary

They cannot reproduce their own duplicates.txt two weeks later.

docs.title: Task
docs.text:
Write audit.md (900–1100 words) plus any scripts, containing:

  1. Failure analysis. Identify at least five distinct reproducibility or correctness defects in the snippet. For each: the defect, the concrete failure scenario, and the minimal fix. Candidates worth considering include wildcard expansion order, cat of gzipped files, cut on FASTQ header semantics, memory behaviour of sort, output paths outside the project, absence of pinned tool versions, missing checksums, and locale-dependent sorting.
  2. Corrected workflow. Provide a workflow/ directory with:
  3. pipeline.yml (bioflow schema) or a Snakefile if you prefer — state which and why;
  4. a README.md stating inputs, outputs and how to verify success;
  5. run.sh that fails fast (set -euo pipefail) and logs tool versions to versions.txt.
  6. Verification. Demonstrate that running your workflow twice produces identical outputs (hash them), and that changing one input changes exactly the expected outputs.
  7. Honest limits. Two paragraphs on what your audit cannot detect (e.g. wrong biological assumptions, batch effects, contamination).

docs.title: Deliverables
docs.text:
audit.md
workflow/{pipeline.yml|Snakefile, run.sh, README.md}
evidence/{hashes_before.txt, hashes_after.txt, versions.txt, rerun_diff.txt}

docs.title: Rubric (20 points)
docs.text: Criterion Points Five defects, each with scenario + fix (2 each) 10 Corrected workflow runs from clean state 3 Determinism evidenced by hashes 3 Tool-version capture 1 Honest limitations 2 Writing clarity (no unquantified claims) 1

docs.title: Reproducibility requirement
docs.text: Your submission must run on a machine that is not yours. Test it in a fresh directory or container before submitting; state in audit.md that you did so and what broke.

docs.title: Extension (bonus, 3 points)
docs.text: Add a GitHub Actions workflow that runs your corrected pipeline on push and fails if outputs change unexpectedly. Include the badge.

docs.title: Challenge 01 — A streaming QC tool that survives real files
docs.text: Level: L4 (challenge) · Time: 6–8 hours · Prerequisites: Modules 1–2, practicals 01–02

docs.title: Problem statement
docs.text: bioflow stats currently loads one record at a time (good) but stores all lengths in a list to compute N50 and the length histogram (fine for teaching, wrong for 10⁹ reads). Your task: extend the tool so that it computes correct statistics on inputs it cannot hold in memory, and prove it.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
1. Streaming N50 without storing all lengths. Implement an exact algorithm using a bounded-memory structure (e.g. a fixed-width histogram over log-spaced length bins plus an exact correction, or an external merge sort). State the memory bound as a function of bin count.
  2. Truth test. Write a property-based or randomised test comparing your streaming N50 against the exact in-memory implementation on ≥1000 random length distributions, including heavy-tailed ones. Report the maximum absolute error (must be 0 for an exact algorithm).
  3. Robustness. Handle correctly:
  4. a file with no trailing newline;
  5. a truncated final FASTQ record (must raise a clear error naming the record index);
  6. a gzip file whose stream is truncated mid-record;
  7. a file containing CRLF line endings.
  8. Performance evidence. Generate a 500 MB synthetic FASTQ (scripts/ may be extended) and report wall time and peak RSS for your implementation versus the current one. Peak RSS must not grow with input size — show the numbers.
  9. Integration. Add bioflow stats --streaming (or a new subcommand) with the same JSON schema, and update docs/modules/01-unix-mindset.md §6 to mention it honestly.

docs.title: Deliverables
docs.text:
• src/bioflow/<yourmodule>.py with docstrings stating complexity and memory bounds.
  • tests/test_<yourmodule>.py — must run in CI in <120 s.
  • CHALLENGE_01_REPORT.md: design, memory bound derivation, error measurements, performance table, and a "what I would do differently at 10¹¹ reads" paragraph.
  • A pull-request-style diff summary.

docs.title: Rubric (30 points)
docs.text: Criterion Points Algorithm correct and exact (verified by the 1000-case test) 8 Memory bound derived, not asserted 5 Robustness cases all handled with clear errors 6 Performance evidence measured (not estimated) 5 Integration quality: schema compatible, docs updated 3 Report honesty (limitations stated) 3

docs.title: Hard constraints
docs.text:
• No new runtime dependency for the core algorithm (standard library only).
  • No silent fallbacks: if the streaming path cannot be exact, it must say so and use the exact path.
  • Any approximation must be labelled in the JSON output (e.g. "n50_method": "exact" | "approximate").

docs.title: Why this is hard
docs.text: The temptation is to check the length histogram rather than the cumulative distribution, which gives a subtly wrong N50 for heavy-tailed assemblies — exactly the case where N50 is used as a headline statistic. A wrong N50 is worse than an absent one, because it gets quoted in papers.

docs.title: Level-1 knowledge quiz — Module 1 (with answer key)
docs.text:
Instructor note: this quiz is diagnostic, not gatekeeping. 12 questions, 15 minutes, closed-book. Answer key at the end — remove it before distributing.

  1. What are the three standard streams, and which file descriptor numbers are they?
  2. Explain the difference between > and >> in one sentence each.
  3. A FASTQ record consists of how many lines, and what is each line?
  4. Why can grep -c '^@' over-count FASTQ records?
  5. Give the Phred score corresponding to a per-base error probability of 1 in 1000.
  6. Define N50 in words, then as an algorithm.
  7. In awk 'NR%4==2 {…}', what does NR%4==2 select, and why is this only valid for single-line FASTQ?
  8. What does gsub(/G/,"") do to $0, and what consequence does that have for length($0)?
  9. Why is a pipe's memory use independent of file size, but a sort in the middle of the pipe is not?
  10. Name three properties a workflow file should record that a shell history does not.
  11. What is the scientific problem with reporting a GC content that includes ambiguous bases in the denominator?
  12. Your pipeline reports "0 executed, 4 skipped" on a re-run. Give one benign and one worrying explanation.

docs.title: Answer key
docs.text:
1. stdin (0), stdout (1), stderr (2).
  2. > truncates the destination before running the command; >> appends.
  3. Four: header (@id description), sequence, + separator, quality string (one ASCII char per base).
  4. Because quality characters use Phred+33 over ASCII 33–126, which includes @ (ASCII 64); a quality line may therefore begin with @.
  5. Q30 (10^(−30/10) = 10⁻³).
  6. In words: the length such that contigs of at least that length cover ≥50% of the assembly. As an algorithm: sort lengths descending; accumulate; the first length at which the cumulative sum reaches ≥ half the total is the N50.
  7. Selects lines 2, 6, 10, … — the sequence lines of consecutive 4-line records. Valid only when no record wraps.
  8. It deletes all G characters from the current record, so a later length($0) measures the line after deletion — under-counting the denominator (our buggy GC = 152%).
  9. A pipe moves data through a fixed kernel buffer; sort must hold (essentially) all input before emitting the first line, so its memory scales with input.
  10. Any three of: tool versions; declared inputs and outputs; checksums of inputs; parameters; environment; derived dependency order; provenance log.
  11. Including N in the denominator dilutes GC%, so a high-N draft assembly looks AT-rich — biasing exactly the QC decision you are making.
  12. Benign: nothing changed since the last run, so caching is correct. Worrying: outputs were deleted or an input path changed silently (e.g. a symlink), so the pipeline believes it is up to date when it is not — verify with ls/hashes.

docs.title: Marking
docs.text: 1 point each; 10–12 pass, 7–9 needs review of §4 of the module, ≤6 re-read the module before attempting Practical 02.

docs.title: Alignment
docs.text: Each question maps to a learning objective: 1–3, 9 → LO1/L2; 4, 7, 8 → LO3; 5, 6, 11 → LO2/L4; 10, 12 → LO5. Questions 6, 11, 12 are deliberately the ones that separate "remembered commands" from "understands data".

docs.title: Instructor pack — Linux, Git and Reproducible Workflows for Bioinformatics
docs.text: This pack exists because the evidence says instructors — not students — are the bottleneck in bioinformatics education: lack of faculty training (24%) and lack of vetted teaching materials were the top two reported barriers in a 1,264-respondent survey (Williams et al., bioRxiv 204420). Everything here is designed so you can teach from it without having written it.

docs.title: What you can adopt, and how long it takes
docs.text:
Format Content Contact hours Prep (first delivery) Marking load Workshop (12 h) Modules 1–2 + Practicals 1–2 12 2 h (run the notebook once) none (formative) Short course (24 h) Modules 1–5 + Practicals 1–2 + Assignment 1 24 4 h ~15 min/student Full course (36 h) Modules 1–9 + all assessment + capstone 36 8 h ~35 min/student

Module 2–9 lessons are specified but not yet written (see docs/roadmap.md); before Module 1 ships in a 24-hour format, allow the dates in the roadmap to be checked.

docs.title: Three things learners get wrong, every time
docs.text:
1. Reporting a count without knowing its method. They will run grep -c '^@' and report 204 confidently. Do not correct it immediately — ask them to reconcile with wc -l / 4. The reconciliation is the lesson.
  2. Believing that a pipeline that runs is a pipeline that is correct. Introduce a step whose declared output it never writes; bioflow fails loudly (see test_step_that_forgets_its_outputs_is_a_failure). Ask why silent success is more dangerous than an error.
  3. Confusing "mean quality" (three different quantities). Use the per_position vs per_read vs overall distinction in Practical 02. Make them say which one they mean, every time.

docs.title: Equipment and access notes
docs.text:
• Minimum: any laptop with Linux, macOS or WSL2, Python ≥3.10, no GPU, no admin rights beyond a venv. Everything runs offline after install.
  • Bandwidth: the whole repository is under 1 MB; installed dependencies are ~50 MB. There is no large download in the graded path.
  • No account required for any exercise. GitHub is used only in Module 6, where an account is necessary; that module must remain optional for grading.
  • CI alternative: if local installs are impossible, notebooks/01_unix_mindset.ipynb runs in a free Colab instance.

docs.title: Assessment design
docs.text:
• Levels 1–2 are formative: quiz + guided practicals, self-marked with the answer key.
  • Level 3 (assignment) is the first summative item; rubric in docs/assessments/assignment-01-shell-audit.md.
  • Level 5 (capstone) requires a public repository; grading must not require public posting — accept a private repo export if a learner declines to publish.
  • Academic-integrity note: the material is CC BY 4.0, so learners may reuse it. Ask them to cite the release they used; do not require a citation to this project in exchange for marks.

docs.title: Adapting the material
docs.text:
• Fork the repository and keep your changes in a branch per cohort; this keeps your teaching version stable.
  • Replace the simulated datasets with your own instrument data — the notebooks read paths from datasets/sample/, so a new directory plus a metadata/*.yml file is enough.
  • If your course is in another language, the content licence (CC BY 4.0) permits translation with attribution; please open an issue so we can link your version.

docs.title: Feedback to the maintainers
docs.text: Content errors: use the "Content error" issue template, quoting the file and line. Adoption reports ("I taught this to N students, here is what broke") are the most valuable contribution you can make and are explicitly welcomed in CONTRIBUTING.md.

docs.title: Module 1 — The Unix mindset: files, pipes and biological text
docs.text: Level: beginner · Time: 3–4 hours · Dataset: datasets/sample/reads.fastq (200 simulated reads), datasets/sample/proteins.fasta, datasets/sample/contigs.fasta Executable companion: notebooks/01_unix_mindset.ipynb — every number below is reproduced there by CI.

docs.title: 1. Scientific background
docs.text:
Almost every file you will touch as a computational biologist is a line-oriented text file: FASTA, FASTQ, GFF3, VCF, SAM, BED, Newick, PDB. The format families differ, but they share a design decision made in the 1970s: one record per line, or a fixed number of lines per record, delimited by characters rather than length fields. That decision is why a 40 GB FASTQ can be inspected with head and filtered with grep in constant memory, and why the Unix toolkit remains, fifty years later, the most reliable interface to biological data.

This matters scientifically rather than aesthetically. The reproducibility literature names compute-environment and process control as a pillar of reproducible research (Pillar 3 and Pillar 5 in Naylor et al.'s "five pillars", Briefings in Bioinformatics 2023, doi:10.1093/bib/bbad375). A result produced by commands typed into a terminal and never recorded is not reproducible — even when the numbers are right. So the goal of this module is not "learn 30 commands". It is: be able to state, in a file you can re-run, exactly how a number was produced.

docs.title: 2. Learning objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this module you can:

  1. Explain the difference between a file, a stream and a pipe, and predict when a command will stream rather than load data into memory.
  2. Compose head, wc, grep, sort, uniq, cut and awk into a one-line quality check, and say what each component does.
  3. Identify and demonstrate a specific class of counting error (heuristic line arithmetic vs parsing) and justify which you used.
  4. Write a command whose output you can validate against a second, independent implementation.
  5. Explain why a pipeline should be a file describing required outputs rather than a shell history, and read a bioflow plan DAG.

docs.title: 3. Required software
docs.text:
# from the repository root
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate    # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -e ".[dev]"
bioflow --version        # expect: bioflow 0.1.0

POSIX tools (head, wc, grep, awk, sort) are present on Linux and macOS. On Windows use WSL2 — not Git Bash, and not "install GNU tools and hope". Module 1 assumes a POSIX shell; pretending otherwise causes exactly the silent failures described in §9.

docs.title: 4.1 Files, streams, pipes
docs.text:
A program started from a shell receives three open channels: stdin (fd 0), stdout (fd 1), stderr (fd 2). A pipe | connects one program's stdout to the next program's stdin.

head -400 reads.fastq | wc -l        # 400 lines pass through, nothing is written to disk

The scientific consequence is scale independence of your attention: you can profile a dataset you cannot fit in RAM, and you can stop a computation early (head) without paying for it.

Two operators you must distinguish:

Operator Meaning Failure mode if confused > redirect stdout to a file, truncating it first grep x big.txt > big.txt destroys big.txt before grep reads it >> append repeated runs silently duplicate results

docs.title: 4.2 Why line structure is a contract
docs.text:
FASTQ is exactly four lines per record:

@header            <- '@' + identifier + optional description
SEQUENCE           <- A/C/G/T/N, no spaces
+                  <- separator, optionally repeating the header
QUALITY            <- one ASCII character per base

Because it is four lines, wc -l / 4 gives the record count. Because the quality alphabet (Phred+33, ASCII 33–126) can contain @, counting lines beginning with @ over-counts. This is not a theoretical worry: in our own 200-read simulated dataset, grep -c '^@' returns 204 — four quality lines begin with @. The notebook demonstrates it.

The general principle is worth stating explicitly, because it recurs in every module:

A heuristic (line arithmetic, filename conventions, "it usually looks like this") is fast and usually right. A parser (a stated grammar, validated case by case) is slower and sometimes right in ways the heuristic is not. Never mix the two without saying which you used.

docs.title: 4.3 Composition and quality, defined rather than assumed
docs.text:
• GC content here is (G + C) / (A + T + G + C). Ambiguous symbols (N, R, Y, …) are excluded from both numerator and denominator. Including them silently deflates GC content in draft assemblies — a classic source of irreproducible QC numbers.
  • Phred score Q maps to per-base error probability P = 10^(−Q/10): Q20 = 1%, Q30 = 0.1%. A "Q30 filter" is therefore a statement about expected errors, not a magic number.

docs.title: 4.4 From commands to a pipeline
docs.text:
A shell history answers "what did I type?". A pipeline answers "what must exist, and what produces it?". bioflow reads YAML where each step declares inputs and outputs; the execution order is derived from those paths, and up-to-date steps are skipped using SHA-256 of inputs plus the command string.

steps:
  - name: qc_reads
    command: bioflow stats {inputs} --json > {outputs}
    inputs: [datasets/sample/reads.fastq]
    outputs: [results/qc/reads.json]

docs.title: 5. Mathematical and computational foundations
docs.text:
Record count from line count, for a well-formed single-line FASTQ:

\[ n_\text{records} = \frac{L}{4}, \qquad L = \text{number of newline-terminated lines} \]

Mean per-position quality over n reads at position i:

\[ \bar{Q}_i = \frac{1}{n_i}\sum_{k=1}^{n_i} Q_{k,i}, \qquad n_i = \#\{\text{reads with length} > i\} \]

Expected number of erroneous bases in a read of length m:

\[ E[\text{errors}] = \sum_{j=1}^{m} 10^{-Q_j/10} \]

That last formula is why two reads with the same mean Q can have different error counts — mean quality is not a sufficient statistic. We return to this in Module 7 and in the capstone.

Cost model of a pipe: each stage adds one process and one copy through a 64 KiB kernel buffer. xargs -P or a workflow manager buys parallelism; a longer pipe does not.

docs.title: 6. Practical demonstration
docs.text:
cd /path/to/linux-git-for-bioinformatics

# 1. What is in the file?
head -4 datasets/sample/reads.fastq

# 2. How many records? (two ways — they will disagree, deliberately)
wc -l < datasets/sample/reads.fastq        # 800 -> 200 records
grep -c '^@' datasets/sample/reads.fastq   # 204  <- over-counts: quality lines can start with '@'

# 3. Composition, computed by an independent implementation
awk 'NR%4==2 {n+=length($0); g+=gsub(/[Gg]/,""); c+=gsub(/[Cc]/,"")} END {printf "%.4f\n", (g+c)/n}' \
    datasets/sample/reads.fastq            # 0.6040

# 4. The library, for comparison
bioflow stats datasets/sample/reads.fastq

# 5. A pipeline you can re-run
bioflow plan examples/pipeline.yml
bioflow run  examples/pipeline.yml         # 4 executed
bioflow run  examples/pipeline.yml         # 0 executed, 4 skipped

docs.title: 7. Expected output
docs.text:
$ bioflow stats datasets/sample/reads.fastq
file            : datasets/sample/reads.fastq
records         : 200
total bases     : 12000
GC              : 60.4%  (ambiguous bases excluded)
length min/mean/max : 60 / 60.0 / 60
N50             : 60
mean Phred      : 30.46

$ bioflow run examples/pipeline.yml
run : qc_reads
run : qc_contigs
run : contig_lengths
run : combine
ok: 4 executed, 0 skipped

and results/contig_lengths.txt:

>contig_1 synthetic=True
47
>contig_2 synthetic=True
56
>contig_3 synthetic=True
120

docs.title: 8. Interpretation of results
docs.text:
• GC = 60.4% matches the simulation parameters (a GC-rich synthetic "genome"), which is the only thing it can legitimately be checked against. On real data you would compare against the reference genome's GC and against a negative control — a 60% GC in a species whose genome is 41% GC is a contamination signal, not a curiosity.
  • Mean Phred 30.46 means roughly three expected errors per 60 bp read by E[errors] = Σ 10^(−Q/10) — not "30.46 correct bases per 100".
  • The two record counts differ (200 vs 204) and that difference is the lesson: the heuristic over-counts by exactly the number of quality lines beginning with @. If you cannot explain a discrepancy, you have not finished the analysis.
  • 0 executed, 4 skipped on the second run is a reproducibility signal: the pipeline knows its outputs are current because it fingerprints its inputs. If it re-ran everything, either an input changed or your tool is not checking the right thing.

docs.title: 9. Common errors and troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix grep -c '^@' ≠ wc -l / 4 Quality lines starting with @ (or wrapped FASTQ) Use a parser; treat the discrepancy as information GC > 100% gsub() mutates $0, so length($0) afterwards excludes G/C Compute lengths before substitutions — this exact bug was found while building this lesson bioflow: command not found Package not installed in the active environment pip install -e . inside the venv; check which python Pipeline re-runs everything each time Inputs are regenerated with a new timestamp/hash upstream Fingerprint content, not mtime; check .bioflow/stamps/ bioflow run fails with "unsatisfiable inputs" A step names an input nothing produces and which does not exist Fix the path, or add the producing step; run bioflow plan first awk: syntax error inside a pipeline Shell quoting: the command is passed to sh, so single-quote the awk program Use '{...}'; see docs/limitations.md on brace handling Windows: tools missing No POSIX shell Use WSL2 (recommended) or a container

docs.title: 10. Exercises
docs.text:
See docs/practicals/practical-01-counting-and-composition.md and practical-02-pipes-and-streams.md for the guided versions; independent work is in docs/assessments/.

Quick self-check (answers in the notebook, not here): 1. Why is sort | uniq -c preferred to a Python Counter for a 40 GB file? 2. What does wc -l count if the last line has no trailing newline? 3. Which of the two record counts would you report to a collaborator, and how would you justify it?

docs.title: 11. Further reading and references
docs.text:
• Cock, P.J.A. et al. (2010) "The Sanger FASTQ file format for sequences with quality scores, and the Solexa/Illumina FASTQ variants." Nucleic Acids Research 38(6):1767–1771. doi:10.1093/nar/gkp1137 — the normative FASTQ description used above.
  • Naylor, B. et al. (2023) "The five pillars of computational reproducibility: bioinformatics and beyond." Briefings in Bioinformatics 24(6):bbad375. doi:10.1093/bib/bbad375 — the reproducibility framework this repository enforces.
  • GNU Coreutils manual — head, wc, sort, uniq, cut semantics and edge cases.
  • POSIX awk specification (The Open Group Base Specifications) — gsub, NR, field splitting.
  • Software Carpentry The Unix Shell lesson — an excellent, longer treatment of the same fundamentals; this module assumes its existence and does not duplicate it.
  • Waskom, M. (2021) "seaborn: statistical data visualization." JOSS 6(60):3021. doi:10.21105/joss.03021 — for Module 3's figures (listed here because the quality plot is your first QC figure).

All references verified against Crossref on 2026-11-06; see docs/references.md for the verification log.

docs.title: Practical 01 — Counting and composition on real file structure
docs.text: Module: 1 · Level: L2 (guided practical) · Time: 45 min · Dataset: datasets/sample/reads.fastq

docs.title: Aim
docs.text: Produce three numbers about a FASTQ file — record count, GC fraction, mean read length — by two independent routes (POSIX tools, then bioflow), and reconcile any disagreement.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
Work in a scratch directory. Keep a file practical01.sh containing every command you run, in order, with set -euo pipefail at the top. At the end, run bash practical01.sh > practical01_output.txt 2>&1 — that file is what you submit.

  1. Inspect before computing. Print the first four lines. State in one sentence what each line is.
  2. Count records two ways. wc -l and grep -c '^@'. Record both numbers.
  3. Explain the difference. Find which lines are being over-counted: 
    awk 'NR%4==0 && /^@/ {print NR": "$0}' datasets/sample/reads.fastq | head
    Write one sentence explaining, in terms of the FASTQ specification, why this happens.
  4. GC fraction. Compute with awk (see Module 1 §6). Then compute with bioflow stats --json and compare to 4 decimal places.
  5. Deliberately break it. Run the buggy variant from the notebook (length($0) after the substitutions). Record the impossible value you get and explain the mechanism.
  6. Mean read length. One-liner it. Confirm against bioflow stats.

docs.title: Deliverables
docs.text:
1. practical01.sh (re-runnable, no hard-coded absolute paths).
  2. practical01_output.txt.
  3. A 150–200 word note answering: which record count would you report, and what would you tell a collaborator who asked "why do I get 204?"

docs.title: Rubric (10 points)
docs.text: Criterion Points What earns full marks Script runs end-to-end from a clean shell 2 set -euo pipefail; no absolute paths; idempotent Both counting methods, with explanation 2 Correctly identifies Phred+33 @ as the cause GC cross-check 2 Agreement stated to 4 dp with the exact values Bug reproduction + mechanism 2 Explains gsub mutating $0, not merely "it was wrong" Written judgement 2 Clear, quantified, no hedging without a number

docs.title: Common wrong answers (instructor note)
docs.text:
• "204 because of the + line" — no: check which lines are matched.
  • Reporting grep -c as the record count without comment.
  • Comparing GC by eye ("about 60%") instead of stating tolerance.

docs.title: Extension
docs.text: Repeat for proteins.fasta. FASTA has no quality lines — predict whether the two methods agree, then test your prediction. If they disagree, why?

docs.title: Practical 02 — Pipes, streams and constant memory
docs.text: Module: 1 · Level: L2 (guided practical) · Time: 45 min · Dataset: datasets/sample/reads.fastq

docs.title: Aim
docs.text: Demonstrate — not assert — that a pipe processes data without loading it into memory, and that a pipeline file can replace a shell history.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
1. Measure, don't assume. Compare peak memory of two ways to find the longest read: 

    /usr/bin/time -v awk 'NR%4==2 {if (length($0)>m) m=length($0)} END{print m}' datasets/sample/reads.fastq 2>&1 | grep -E "Maximum resident|^[0-9]+"
    Then do the same with a Python list comprehension that materialises every read. Record both peak-RSS figures. (On macOS use /usr/bin/time -l; state which you used.)

  2. Build a stream. Write a single pipeline that prints the number of reads whose mean Phred is below 30, using only POSIX tools (awk, no Python). Hint: compute per-read mean quality from line 4, compare, count.

  3. Verify against the library. Confirm your number with bioflow stats --json (compute per-read means from per_position_mean_quality? No — that is per position; explain why your POSIX answer cannot be reproduced from that field, then write three lines of Python that compute the per-read means properly).

  4. Truncation hazards. Create test.txt with three lines. Run grep -v zzz test.txt > test.txt. Explain what you observe and why (> truncates before the left side reads).

  5. Make it a pipeline. Write practical02.yml with three steps:

  6. per_read_quality → results/per_read.txt
  7. low_quality_count → results/low_quality_count.txt (depends on the first)
  8. summary → results/summary.txt (depends on both) Run bioflow plan before bioflow run, and run twice to prove caching.

docs.title: Deliverables
docs.text:
1. A markdown report with the two peak-RSS numbers, the pipeline one-liner, the verification numbers, and the truncation explanation.
  2. practical02.yml, plus bioflow plan output.
  3. One paragraph: why does the streaming version use less memory, in terms of the kernel buffer and process lifetimes?

docs.title: Rubric (10 points)
docs.text: Criterion Points What earns full marks Memory measurement actually performed 2 Numbers reported, method and platform named POSIX-only pipeline works 2 Correct handling of quality line; no Python Verification, including the per-position vs per-read distinction 3 Recognises that per_position_mean_quality is a different quantity Truncation behaviour explained 1 Mentions shell opening order Pipeline YAML valid and cached on second run 2 bioflow plan clean; second run reports skips

docs.title: Note on per_position_mean_quality
docs.text: This is the most common conceptual error in FASTQ QC: per_position_mean_quality[i] is the mean over reads at position i — useful for trimming decisions. The mean of a single read is a different statistic, and the mean of all bases (what bioflow stats reports as mean_quality) is a third. Three quantities, three meanings, one ambiguous phrase ("mean quality"). Say which you mean.

docs.title: Tutorial 01 — Your first pipeline (15 minutes)
docs.text: Goal: turn three commands into a pipeline file, then prove it is reproducible.

docs.title: Step 1 — Do it by hand
docs.text:
mkdir -p results
bioflow stats datasets/sample/reads.fastq --json > results/reads.json
bioflow stats datasets/sample/contigs.fasta --json > results/contigs.json

Two files exist. Nothing about this is reproducible yet: the commands live in your shell history.

docs.title: Step 2 — Write the pipeline
docs.text:
Create my_first_pipeline.yml:

steps:
  - name: qc_reads
    command: bioflow stats {inputs} --json > {outputs}
    inputs: [datasets/sample/reads.fastq]
    outputs: [results/reads.json]

  - name: qc_contigs
    command: bioflow stats {inputs} --json > {outputs}
    inputs: [datasets/sample/contigs.fasta]
    outputs: [results/contigs.json]

docs.title: Step 3 — Ask what it will do before it does it
docs.text:
bioflow plan my_first_pipeline.yml

Read the output. If the order surprises you, the bug is in your inputs/outputs, not in the tool.

docs.title: Step 4 — Run it, twice
docs.text:
bioflow run my_first_pipeline.yml
bioflow run my_first_pipeline.yml

Second run: 0 executed, 2 skipped.

docs.title: Step 5 — Break it on purpose
docs.text:
Change one byte in datasets/sample/contigs.fasta (add a blank line at the end) and run again. Exactly one step should re-run. Now revert the file and run again — both steps re-run, because the content changed back and the stamp records the content it saw.

This is the whole idea: the pipeline's memory is a fingerprint of reality, not a timestamp.

docs.title: Step 6 — Inspect the provenance
docs.text:
cat bioflow_run.log
cat .bioflow/stamps/qc_reads.json

The stamp contains the command, the completion time, and a SHA-256 of every output. That file is what a reviewer would ask for.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:

  • Challenge 01 asks you to make the statistics themselves memory-bounded.
